meta.title: Who really said "Every individual is an exception to the rule"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Jung — but not from his famous 1921 book. It is on page 295 of his 1925 essay "Psychological Types." And a reviewer wrote it first, in 1906.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every individual is an exception to the rule'?
meta.ogDescription: Jung wrote it in a 1925 Morton Prince festschrift, from his 1923 Territet lecture — not in Psychological Types (1921). Quote Investigator found a 1906 version.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist, founder of analytical psychology
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Jung — but not from the book almost everyone cites. The sentence sits on page 295 of his essay “Psychological Types,” a paper read at the International Congress of Education in Territet, Switzerland in 1923 and printed in the 1925 Morton Prince festschrift Problems of Personality. Quote Investigator adds the important caveat: an anonymous Edinburgh Review critic wrote a near-identical line in April 1906, so Jung popularised the saying rather than coined it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Psychological Types,” in Problems of Personality: Studies Presented to Dr. Morton Prince
1925 · Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., London · article pp. 289–295, quotation on p. 295
Paper read at the International Congress of Education, Territet, Switzerland, 1923
English as printed in the 1925 volume; the 1928 reprint in Contributions to Analytical Psychology used H. G. and Cary F. Baynes’s translation

source.excerpt: Although there are without a doubt individuals in whom one can recognise the type at a first glance, for the most part this is by no means the case. As a rule only careful observation and a weighing of the evidence permits a sure classification. Clear and simple though the fundamental principle of the two opposing attitudes may be, nevertheless their concrete reality is complicated and obscure, for every individual is an exception to the rule. Therefore, one can never give a description of a type, no matter how complete, which applies to more than one individual despite the fact that thousands might, in a certain sense, be strikingly described thereby. Conformity is one side of a man, uniqueness is the other.
trail: Quote Investigator traced the line to Jung’s 1925 article “Psychological Types” in Problems of Personality (start page 289, quote page 295), noting the citation was verified with scans, and states the quotation appeared in neither the German nor the English translation of the 1921 book.

We confirmed it directly in the Internet Archive scan of the 1925 Kegan Paul volume: the clause “for every individual is an exception to the rule” falls under the running head “PSYCHOLOGICAL TYPES 295,” and the article opens on page 289 with the footnote “Paper read at the International Congress of Education.”
The same sentence reappears on page 303 of Contributions to Analytical Psychology, whose contents page lists the piece as a lecture given at the International Congress of Education at Territet, 1923.

Quote Investigator also records an anonymous reviewer in The Edinburgh Review, April 1906 (vol. 203, quote page 364), writing “In human life every individual is an exception to rules” — and conjectures the remark has been constructed multiple times independently.
source.excerptNote: The famous clause is a subordinate one — Jung wrote it as a warning label on his own typology, not as a standalone aphorism. The 1928 Baynes reprint revises the sentences around it (“which absolutely applies to one individual… strikingly characterized by it”) while keeping the key clause word for word.

author.name: Carl Jung
author.heading: About Carl Jung
author.metaLine: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist & founder of analytical psychology
author.bio: Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology after breaking with Freud, and who gave ordinary speech the words introvert and extravert. His 1921 book Psychologische Typen laid out the typology — two attitudes crossed with four functions — that was later commercialised as the Myers-Briggs test. This sentence is Jung supplying his own warning label: the moment he had built the categories, he insisted they described averages and not people.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Jung holds up. What almost every reposting gets wrong is where he wrote it — and whether he thought of it first.

items.why: The line is routinely credited to Jung’s famous 1921 book. Quote Investigator checked and states the quotation appeared in neither the German nor the English translation of the 1921 book. It comes from a lecture that carried the same title — “Psychologische Typen” / “Psychological Types” — delivered in 1923 and printed in 1925. The title collision is the whole reason for the confusion.

Quote Investigator found an unnamed book reviewer in The Edinburgh Review of April 1906 writing “In human life every individual is an exception to rules, the more exceptional as his or her individuality is more strongly marked.” QI’s conclusion is that Jung should be credited with popularising the statement, and that at least one person crafted it before him.

The follow-on sentence circulates in a modernised form. Jung’s printed English reads “Conformity is one side of a man, uniqueness is the other” — identically in the 1925 volume and in the 1928 Baynes reprint.

misattribution.truthLine: He really wrote it — on page 295 of a 1925 festschrift for Morton Prince, from a lecture given in Territet in 1923. Not in the 1921 book, and, on Quote Investigator’s evidence, not first.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Jung is usually quoted here as if he were being warmly humanist. He was actually being self-critical. He had just spent a book sorting humanity into two attitudes — extraverted and introverted — crossed with four functions: sensation, thinking, feeling and intuition. Standing in front of an audience of educators at Territet in 1923, he attached the caveat: the scheme describes an average, and the average person is nobody. “The individual soul is not explained by classification,” the passage goes on.

That caveat has outlived most of the typology. It is the sentence people reach for whenever a personality test starts sounding too certain of itself — Quote Investigator notes that Malcolm Gladwell used it in a 2004 New Yorker piece on the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, presenting Jung’s own scepticism about slotting people into categories.
context.detailsSummary: Why the 1921 book keeps getting the credit
detailsBody: Jung gave a lecture and a book the same name. The book, Psychologische Typen, was published by Rascher Verlag in 1921 and translated into English by H. Godwyn Baynes; the lecture, delivered to the International Congress of Education at Territet in 1923, summarised the book’s argument for a general audience and was printed in English in 1925.

Because the two share a title, quotation collections file the sentence under the book — where, per Quote Investigator, it does not appear. The 1925 printing is the first place it can be read in English, in a volume assembled to honour the American psychopathologist Morton Prince.
